paras.text: SN1 stands for Substitution, Nucleophilic, unimolecular. It is a two-step mechanism. First step is slow (rate determining or rate limiting step) and involves the formation of intermediate carbocation by dissociation of alkyl halide or substrate. The term unimolecular means there is only one molecule involved in transition state of the rate-determing step. The second step is fast and involves the attack of nucleophile on planar carbocation and formation of product. SN1 mechanism is generally followed by tertiary alkyl halides. As it involves the formation of carbocation, it is favored by highly ionizing polar solvents (having O–H, N–H bond). For example the hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide follow SN1 mechanism as shown below.

Carbocations are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary according to the number of carbons (alkyl groups) that are directly attached to the positively charged carbon. Primary alkyl halides produce primary carbocations while secondary and tertiary alkyl halides yield secondary and tertiary carbocations respectively.

Alkyl groups directly attached to the positively charged carbon stabilize a carbocation, through its electron donating effect. Thus tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary and secondary are more stable than primary ones. This stabilization comes from the stabilization of the positive charge of the carbocation by the electron donating alkyl groups directly attached. (Figure 17.3)

Mechanisms of Nucleophilic Substitution reactions

Alkyl halides can undergo nucleophilic substitution by two different types of mechanisms. The type of mechanism depends upon the nature of alkyl halides.

17.1.6.3 SN1 Mechanism

SN1 stands for Substitution, Nucleophilic, unimolecular. It is a two-step mechanism. First step is slow (rate determining or rate limiting step) and involves the formation of intermediate carbocation by dissociation of alkyl halide or substrate. The term unimolecular means there is only one molecule involved in transition state of the rate-determing step. The second step is fast and involves the attack of nucleophile on planar carbocation and formation of product. SN1 mechanism is generally followed by tertiary alkyl halides. As it involves the formation of carbocation, it is favored by highly ionizing polar solvents (having O–H, N–H bond). For example the hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide follow SN1 mechanism as shown below.

Step–1: The substrate undergoes ionization and yield a carbocation. The bromine atom completely detaches from the substrate as bromide ion.

Step–2: In second step, the entering nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation on either face, to produce the end product.

The kinetic studies have shown that reactions proceeding through SN1 mechanism follow the first order kinetics. The rate of reaction depends only upon the concentration of substrate. The rate equation for above reaction is; rate = k [(CH₃)₃CBr]

Tidbit

Two transition states are formed in SN1 mechanism. One in first step during formation of intermediate, the other in second step during formation of product from intermediate.

The intermediate carbocation is planar, the nucleophile attack from either side. If a nucleophile attacks the carbocation from the side of the leaving group, the product molecule shows retention of configuration. Attack from the side opposite to leaving group, gives a product molecule showing inversion of configuration. If the reactant is chiral, mixture of two enantiomers (Section 16.6.5) are produced, called racemic mixture and this process is called racemization. Racemization is simply a combination of retention and inversion. However in SN1, the product is rarely completely racemic and there is often more inversion than retention of configuration. This is also called partial racemization.

Carbocations are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary according to the number of carbons (alkyl groups) that are directly attached to the positively charged carbon. Primary alkyl halides produce primary carbocations while secondary and tertiary alkyl halides yield secondary and tertiary carbocations respectively.

Alkyl groups directly attached to the positively charged carbon stabilize a carbocation, through its electron donating effect. Thus tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary and secondary are more stable than primary ones. This stabilization comes from the stabilization of the positive charge of the carbocation by the electron donating alkyl groups directly attached. (Figure 17.3)

Figure 17.3 Realtive stability order of different types of carbocations.

Mechanisms of Nucleophilic Substitution reactions

Alkyl halides can undergo nucleophilic substitution by two different types of mechanisms. The type of mechanism depends upon the nature of alkyl halides.

17.1.6.3 SN1 Mechanism

SN1 stands for Substitution, Nucleophilic, unimolecular. It is a two-step mechanism. First step is slow (rate determining or rate limiting step) and involves the formation of intermediate carbocation by dissociation of alkyl halide or substrate. The term unimolecular means there is only one molecule involved in transition state of the rate-determing step. The second step is fast and involves the attack of nucleophile on planar carbocation and formation of product. SN1 mechanism is generally followed by tertiary alkyl halides. As it involves the formation of carbocation, it is favored by highly ionizing polar solvents (having O–H, N–H bond). For example the hydrolysis of tert-butyl bromide follow SN1 mechanism as shown below.

Step–1: The substrate undergoes ionization and yield a carbocation. The bromine atom completely detaches from the substrate as bromide ion.

Step–2: In second step, the entering nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation on either face, to produce the end product.

The kinetic studies have shown that reactions proceeding through SN1 mechanism follow the first order kinetics. The rate of reaction depends only upon the concentration of substrate. The rate equation for above reaction is; rate = k [(CH₃)₃CBr]

Tidbit

Two transition states are formed in SN1 mechanism. One in first step during formation of intermediate, the other in second step during formation of product from intermediate.

The intermediate carbocation is planar, the nucleophile attack from either side. If a nucleophile attacks the carbocation from the side of the leaving group, the product molecule shows retention of configuration. Attack from the side opposite to leaving group, gives a product molecule showing inversion of configuration. If the reactant is chiral, mixture of two enantiomers (Section 16.6.5) are produced, called racemic mixture and this process is called racemization. Racemization is simply a combination of retention and inversion. However in SN1, the product is rarely completely racemic and there is often more inversion than retention of configuration. This is also called partial racemization.
